newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian government faces bitter budget battle.
newsitem.headline: Russian government faces bitter budget battle.

text.p: Russia's government, still lacking the Kremlin presence of convalescing President Boris Yeltsin, faced bitter battles on several fronts and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told ministers on Thursday to brace for surprises.

Russian news agencies said Chernomyrdin told a cabinet meeting all ministers had to attend a session of the State Duma lower house of parliament on Friday to defend the 1997 budget, which the communist opposition said on Thursday it would block.
"You must be ready for every possibility. Anything could happen," Itar-Tass quoted Chernomyrdin as saying.
The opposition-dominated Duma, which rejected the cabinet's original draft budget, is to discuss a compromise spending plan prepared by a government-parliamentary arbitration commission.
But communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, who met Chernomyrdin on Thursday, said afterwards that his party, the biggest in the Duma, would not accept the revised budget as it stood.
"We've said it before and I said it today, we will not support this budget," Zyuganov told reporters.
Chernomyrdin told his ministers to defend the plan at the session, admitting that "the situation in the economy is very complicated, especially over payment of wages and pensions".

Zyuganov said he did not rule out that the prime minister could make amendments before Friday that would appease the communists, including sacking some ministers. "Everything depends on what we are presented with tomorrow," Zyuganov said.
Conflict between government and Duma might force Yeltsin to make a choice between dismissing one or other of the bodies.
Yeltsin, 65, who had a multiple heart bypass operation on November 5, was spending his first day at a country residence where he moved on Wednesday from the nearby Barvikha sanatorium.

He agreed to meet Bill Clinton next March, probably in the United States, during a telephone conversation with the U.S. president. A Kremlin source told Interfax news agency Yeltsin would soon go on a series of trips around Russia and abroad.
The government is facing angry miners, hundreds of thousands of whom began an indefinite national strike on Tuesday demanding the government be replaced and that Moscow pay overdue wages.

In the biggest coalmining region, the Kuzbass in southern Siberia, the strike appeared to be losing momentum. Yet across Russia, Interfax news agency said, the number of mines on strike grew to 132 on Thursday from 124 on Wednesday.
The Duma passed a resolution on Thursday urging Yeltsin to sort out the mines situation and warning it would hold a no- confidence vote if there were no moves to resolve the conflict.
The Federation Council upper house of parliament summoned a special sitting on December 10 to review Chernomyrdin's record.
On Wednesday, the normally compliant upper house was in uproar against the prime minister after Chernomyrdin, pleading illness, refused to appear to explain his plans for the crisis.
Some Council members, drawn from Russia's regional leaders, had called for a motion of no confidence in the government.
The Council created another headache for Yeltsin on Thursday when it demanded Ukraine hand over the Black Sea naval port of Sevastopol, saying it was Russia's and Kiev had no right to it.
The move is likely to cause a storm of protest in Ukraine and disrupt delicate negotiations between the two governments.

Another problem for Yeltsin is the continuing squabble over land forces commander, General Vladimir Semyonov. Defence Minister Igor Rodionov ordered him sacked last weekend for misconduct but the president has yet to endorse his removal.
Semyonov told Interfax on Thursday Rodionov just wanted an excuse to get rid of him and said he would fight for his honour.
